title: What Is a Project Report and Why Does Your Bank Ask for One?
author: Finthara Team
excerpt: New to business loans? Learn what a project report is, what banks look for in it, and how to prepare a bank-ready report in minutes.
keywords: project report for bank loan, business loan project report, DPR for MSME, how to make project report

blocks.text: You have a business idea, a location in mind and a rough budget. Then the bank manager asks for a project report, and suddenly the loan feels a long way off. The good news: a project report is simply your business plan written in the language a lender understands.
What a project report actually contains

items: **Business overview:** what you will do, where, and who your customers are.
**Project cost:** land, building, machinery, pre-operative expenses and working capital.
**Means of finance:** how much is your contribution and how much is the loan.
**Financial projections:** 5-year profit and loss, cash flow and balance sheet.
**Key ratios:** DSCR, current ratio, break-even and payback period.

blocks.text: Why banks insist on it

A lender is not only judging your idea. It wants evidence that the business can generate enough cash to repay the loan on time. The report is how the bank tests that evidence, so numbers that do not tie together, or ratios that miss the bank's benchmarks, are the most common reasons applications get sent back.

title: CMA Data Explained: The Format Indian Banks Expect
author: Finthara Team
excerpt: CMA data is a must for most business loans in India. Here is what it includes, why banks rely on it, and how to prepare it without errors.
keywords: CMA data format, CMA report for bank loan, credit monitoring arrangement, working capital loan India

blocks.text: If you have applied for a term loan or a cash credit limit in India, you have probably heard the term CMA data. CMA stands for Credit Monitoring Arrangement, and it is the standard set of financial statements banks use to assess how much credit a business can safely handle.
What goes into CMA data

items: Past and projected operating statement (sales, costs and profit).
Analysis of the balance sheet (assets and liabilities, year by year).
Comparative statement of current assets and current liabilities.
Calculation of maximum permissible bank finance (MPBF) for working capital.
Fund flow statement and key ratio analysis.

blocks.text: Why it trips people up

CMA data is not hard because the concepts are complex. It is hard because every figure has to reconcile across several statements. Change the sales assumption in one sheet, and inventory, receivables, working capital and ratios all have to move with it. One mismatch and the credit officer will ask you to redo the file.

title: DSCR, Current Ratio and Payback: The Numbers Banks Check Before Saying Yes
author: Finthara Team
excerpt: Learn the key ratios banks check before approving a business loan, including DSCR, current ratio and payback period, and how to improve them.
keywords: DSCR meaning, debt service coverage ratio, current ratio bank loan, payback period, loan approval ratios

blocks.text: Two businesses can ask for the same loan amount and get very different answers. Often, the difference comes down to a handful of ratios. Understanding them before you apply puts you in control of the conversation.
1. Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR)

DSCR compares the cash your business generates with the loan instalments (principal plus interest) it must pay. A DSCR of 1.5 means you earn ₹1.50 for every ₹1 of debt due. Lenders generally want this comfortably above 1, and many set a minimum around 1.25 or higher.
2. Current Ratio
Current assets divided by current liabilities. It shows whether you can meet short-term obligations. Banks commonly look for roughly 1.33 or better for working-capital lending.
3. Payback Period and IRR
How many years it takes to recover the investment, and the return the project earns. A shorter payback and a healthy IRR signal lower risk.
How to strengthen your numbers

items: Use realistic, sector-appropriate sales and cost assumptions.
Consider a slightly longer repayment tenure or moratorium to ease early-year DSCR.
Increase your own contribution to reduce debt.

title: Applying Under PMEGP or Mudra? Here Is How to Prepare Your Project Report
author: Finthara Team
excerpt: Planning to apply for a PMEGP or Mudra loan? Learn what your project report must include and the mistakes that delay approval.
keywords: PMEGP project report, Mudra loan project report, government loan scheme India, CGTMSE, MSME subsidy

blocks.text: Government-backed schemes such as PMEGP, Mudra and CGTMSE have helped lakhs of Indians start and grow businesses with subsidies, lower collateral requirements or credit guarantees. But every application still goes through a bank, and every bank wants a solid project report.
Schemes at a glance

items: **PMEGP:** a credit-linked subsidy scheme for new micro-enterprises in manufacturing and services.
**Mudra (PMMY):** loans for micro and small businesses across Shishu, Kishore and Tarun categories.
**CGTMSE:** a credit guarantee that helps eligible MSMEs access loans without collateral.

blocks.text: What your report must show

items: A clear description of the activity and why it will succeed locally.
Itemised project cost, including machinery quotes and working capital.
Your own contribution and the loan or subsidy amount requested.
Projections showing the business can repay comfortably.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

Overestimating first-year sales, leaving out working capital, and using a generic template that does not match the scheme's format are the top reasons files get returned. Scheme limits and subsidy rates are also revised from time to time, so always confirm the latest rules on the official portal before applying.
